content: Sesame oil, also known as gingelly oil or til oil, is a vegetable oil extracted from sesame seeds. It is widely used as a cooking oil in South India and as a flavor enhancer in Southeast Asian cuisine. Composition Sesame oil contains various fatty acids, which contribute to its nutritional and functional properties. Historical Context Sesame seeds were among the first crops to be processed for oil and used as condiments. The Tamil word for oil, ennai, originates from the words eL (sesame) and nei (fat). Before 600 BC, the Assyrians used sesame oil as food, a salve, and a medicinal agent, though it was primarily accessible to the wealthy due to its high cost. In Hindu culture, sesame oil is considered sacred and is used in votive lamps. Lighting a lamp filled with sesame oil in front of Lord Hanuman is believed to remove obstacles and difficulties in life. Nomenclature In Tamil, sesame oil is called Nalla Ennai, meaning good oil. In Telugu, it is referred to as Nuvvula Noona, and in Kannada, it is called Yellenne. In India, it is also commonly known as gingelly oil. Manufacturing Process The extraction of sesame oil is labor-intensive and not fully automated. Sesame seeds are encased in capsules that do not open until the seeds are fully ripe. Farmers manually cut the plants and allow them to ripen further before shaking the seeds out. The discovery of a non-shattering sesame variety in 1943 has led to efforts to develop high-yield, shatter-resistant strains, though harvest losses remain a challenge. Sesame is rarely cultivated in industrialized agricultural regions due to the manual labor required. Sesame Seed Market As of 2007, sesame seeds were imported into the United States at a price of $0.43 per pound, reflecting a global shortage. Domestic production in the U.S. is limited by the need for high-yield, non-shattering varieties. Farmers are advised to establish a market before planting sesame crops. Varieties of Sesame Oil Sesame oil varies in color and flavor depending on its processing method. Cold-pressed sesame oil is nearly colorless, while Indian sesame oil is golden, and Chinese sesame oil is dark brown due to the toasting of hulled seeds. Cold-pressed oil has a milder flavor compared to toasted sesame oil. These varieties are traded globally, with cold-pressed oil being popular in Western health stores and hot-pressed oils preferred in Asian countries. Uses of Sesame Oil Cooking Sesame oil is considered more stable than most vegetable oils due to its antioxidant content, which prevents rancidity. It has a high boiling point, allowing it to retain its structure even at high temperatures. It is widely used in Asian cuisines, particularly in Tamil Nadu, where its use is comparable to olive oil in the Mediterranean. Body Massage Sesame oil is known for its ability to penetrate the skin easily and is commonly used in India for oil massages. Hair Treatment Applying sesame oil to the hair is believed to darken it and reduce body heat. It is used for scalp massages and is thought to prevent hair-related issues. Food Manufacturing Sesame oil is used in the production of pickles and margarine in Western countries. Drug Manufacturing In Ayurvedic medicine, sesame oil is a key ingredient in the preparation of various drugs. Worship In Hindu rituals, sesame oil is used in lamps placed before deities. It is also used in temple ceremonies. Industrial Uses Industrially, sesame oil serves as a solvent in injectable drugs and intravenous solutions, a carrier oil in cosmetics, and a coating for stored grains to prevent insect infestations. It also enhances the efficacy of certain insecticides. Alternative Medicine Vitamins and Minerals Sesame oil is a source of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps lower cholesterol. It also contains magnesium, copper, calcium, iron, zinc, and vitamin B6. Copper may alleviate rheumatoid arthritis, magnesium supports vascular and respiratory health, calcium helps prevent colon cancer, osteoporosis, migraines, and PMS, and zinc promotes bone health. Studies on hypertensive rats suggest that sesame lignans inhibit cholesterol synthesis and absorption. Oil Pulling Sesame oil is one of the few oils recommended for oil pulling, an ancient practice believed to improve oral health. Stress and Tension The antioxidants and other compounds in sesame oil are thought to have anti-depressant properties, promoting a sense of well-being and reducing signs of aging. General Claims While not FDA-approved, sesame oil is reputed to have therapeutic benefits. It is believed to alleviate anxiety, nerve and bone disorders, poor circulation, and bowel issues. It is also claimed to relieve fatigue, insomnia, and muscle spasms, and to promote vitality and longevity. Sesame oil is said to restore skin moisture, ease joint dryness, and alleviate symptoms of menopause. Other purported uses include treating toothaches, gum disease, blurred vision, dizziness, and headaches. It is also suggested to have antibacterial properties and potential anti-cancer effects due to its lignan content. Adverse Effects Sesame oil is generally safe when consumed in recommended amounts, but its long-term effects are not well-studied. Caution is advised for children, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and individuals with liver or kidney disease. Due to its laxative properties, it should be avoided by those with diarrhea. The American Heart Association recommends limiting polyunsaturated fat intake, including sesame oil, to no more than 10% of total caloric intake. People allergic to peanuts may also be allergic to sesame seeds and should exercise caution, as sesame allergies can lead to severe reactions, including anaphylaxis.
